title: Controls kept a weighted spring shift estimate near 1.25 days per C in 317 North American bird species
abstract: We tested whether the bird survey spring count-curve shift survives nonlinear climate response, lagged shape controls and shared observation errors. We rebuilt the fixed BBS 2026 release and GHCN_CAMS climate for the 317 species in SCI 314c7ca6. Fits used 8,915,599 species-survey rows in 1966-2024. A free quadratic spring effect and previous and next spring date interactions kept the source variance-weighted estimate at 1.25 days per C, with a conditional 95% interval of 0.94 to 1.55. Corrected weighted same-minus-previous and same-minus-next intervals were 0.81 to 1.76 and 0.81 to 1.73. The planned equal-weight estimate was 0.73, with interval 0.03 to 1.43; its two corrected control contrasts included zero. Shared route and year errors caused little inflation for the source weighted estimator. Opposite-half seasonal curvatures correlated only 0.51. A secondary curve-noise ratio gave 1.43 days per C and a Fieller interval of 0.15 to 3.33 under zero cross-half error covariance. Early-period and June-only records did not give bounded calibration sets. The evidence strengthens the same-spring weighted shape result but does not identify detection, breeding dates or a thermal-trend correction. An exact count-model example shows that availability and seasonal abundance can give the same data. The package includes code, aggregate evidence, figures, source hashes and external-data retrieval. Selection, model shape, estimated weights and approximate uncertainty limit inference.

display.caption: Same-spring shape relations stayed positive under both weight choices. Timing-control contrasts were clear with variance weights and uncertain with equal weights. Intervals include shared route and year score errors.
Seasonal curve noise limited calibration of a common shift. Fieller sets can be unbounded when the cross-half curvature denominator is weak. The ratio requires additional error assumptions.

citations.reason: We rebuild its data and weighted count-curve shape estimate, then add nonlinear climate terms, lagged shape controls, shared scores and ratio uncertainty. The field records overlap fully.
Weak thermal tracking across networks motivates careful separation of seasonal observation effects.
Linear observer drift has a cohort alias. We test a distinct seasonal shape relation and retain mechanism identification limits.
Species-level weak thermal responses motivate a check of the seasonal count response.
Local spatial gradients remain a real benchmark; this study does not re-estimate them.
Habitat explains only part of the spatial-temporal gap.
Hearing-related observation patterns are a separate mechanism; no hearing correction is estimated here.
